docs.title: Microphone Detection Subsystem
docs.text:
Team 203 | Fall 2026

External Design Review — October 26, 2026

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
This individual engineering datasheet documents my design and development work for EGR 304 — Embedded Systems Design at Arizona State University.

My assigned subsystem focuses on detecting and conditioning an audio signal from a microphone so that it can be processed by a PIC18F57Q43 microcontroller.

This website serves as a living engineering document containing the design decisions, component selections, electrical schematics, power calculations, and supporting documentation for the subsystem.

docs.title: Project Overview
docs.text:
The microphone detection subsystem is designed to receive an acoustic signal, condition the signal using analog circuitry, and provide a suitable electrical signal to the microcontroller for processing.

The proposed design includes:

  • A microphone for converting sound into an electrical signal.
  • An MCP6004 operational amplifier for analog signal conditioning.
  • Resistors and capacitors for signal filtering and biasing.
  • A PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board for signal processing.
  • An LM7805 voltage regulator providing a regulated 5 V supply.
  • An external 9–12 V DC power source.

The design is currently in the preliminary development stage. Final component specifications and operating limits will be confirmed through datasheet verification and testing.

docs.title: My Individual Contribution
docs.text:
My responsibilities for the microphone detection subsystem include:

  • Developing and documenting the subsystem block diagram.
  • Researching and evaluating electrical components.
  • Preparing the bill of materials (BOM).
  • Designing the electrical schematic.
  • Developing the preliminary subsystem power budget.
  • Evaluating component compatibility, power requirements, and design constraints.
  • Maintaining engineering documentation for design reviews.

docs.title: System Operation
docs.text:
The intended signal path is:

Acoustic Input → Microphone → Analog Signal Conditioning → PIC18F57Q43 Microcontroller

The microphone produces an electrical signal corresponding to the incoming sound. The analog conditioning circuit amplifies and filters the signal before it reaches the microcontroller.

The microcontroller can then sample the conditioned signal using its analog-to-digital converter (ADC).

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
This block diagram illustrates the major components and signal connections for the Team 203 microphone detection subsystem.

The microphone converts acoustic signals into electrical signals. These signals are conditioned by an MCP6004 operational amplifier circuit before being sent to an analog-to-digital converter (ADC) input on the Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board.

The microcontroller provides digital input/output connections for the pushbutton, indicator LED, and interface connections to other team subsystems.

The proposed power architecture uses an external 9–12 V DC supply and an LM7805 linear voltage regulator to provide a regulated 5 V rail.

The microphone type and final external power supply specifications are pending verification.

docs.title: Component Selection — Microphone Subsystem
docs.text: EGR 304 | Team 203 | Individual subsystem: Microphone

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
The microphone subsystem detects sound for the team's interactive cat-toy project. An analog microphone feeds a signal-conditioning amplifier, which supplies the RA0 ADC input on the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano. The subsystem uses the team's planned 9 V input and regulated 5 V supply.

Components were evaluated for analog interface compatibility, power consumption, PCB integration, cost, and audio performance.

The microphone needs a separate lower-voltage supply; it cannot be connected directly to 5 V.

Design status: The microphone choice is provisional until the schematic, PCB assembly method, and 3.3 V supply are confirmed. Prices are indicative single-unit prices and should be checked before ordering.

docs.title: 1. Microphone Selection
docs.text:
Microphone / Acoustic Sensing

Table 1: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — 3S 3SM121MZB1UA.Analog MEMS, 6-pin LGA; approximately $1.16 each.DigiKey product.Datasheet. 66 dBA SNR• Low 80 µA typical supply current• Single-ended analog output simplifies signal conditioning• Larger body than Option 2. 1.6–3.6 V supply not compatible with direct 5 V• Bottom acoustic port requires PCB opening• LGA package is difficult to hand solder• Additional regulated supply required. Option 2 — 3S 3SM122KZB1VD-002-R.Analog MEMS, 4-pin LGA; approximately $1.06 each.DigiKey product. Very small 2.75 × 1.85 mm footprint• 80 µA typical supply current• Single-ended analog output• Omnidirectional detection. Lower 64 dBA SNR• Requires lower-voltage rail• Small LGA package is difficult to assemble manually• Sensitive to acoustic-port contamination. Option 3 — Syntiant SPH11C3LR5H-1.Differential analog MEMS, 5-pin LGA; approximately $2.12 each.DigiKey product. Best normal-mode SNR of the three (68.5 dBA)• Differential output improves noise rejection• Wide audio frequency response• High acoustic overload tolerance. Higher current (~200–205 µA)• Differential output complicates signal conditioning• 2.4–3.2 V normal-mode supply• Bottom-port LGA requires careful assembly.

docs.title: Selected Microphone
docs.text:
Choice (provisional): Option 1 — 3SM121MZB1UA.

Option 1 balances low supply current and noise performance while retaining a single-ended analog output that can be conditioned by the MCP6004 and sampled by RA0.

Compared with Option 2, it provides 2 dB better SNR for the same typical current. It also avoids the differential-output interface complexity of Option 3.

A regulated 3.3 V microphone supply and appropriate signal-conditioning network must be incorporated into the final design.

docs.title: Electrical Comparison
docs.text:
Characteristic Option 1 Option 2 Option 3 Supply voltage 1.6–3.6 V 1.6–3.6 V 2.4–3.2 V Typical current 80 µA 80 µA 200–205 µA Signal-to-noise ratio 66 dBA 64 dBA 68.5 dBA Sensitivity −38 dBV/Pa −38 dBV/Pa −38 dBV/Pa Output Single-ended Single-ended Differential Dimensions 3.76 × 3.00 × 1.10 mm 2.75 × 1.85 × 0.90 mm 3.50 × 2.65 × 1.00 mm

Datasheet evidence: Option 1, page 4; Option 2, page 4; Option 3, pages 2 and 6.

docs.title: 2. Operational Amplifier / Signal Conditioning
docs.text:
Operational Amplifier / Signal Conditioning

Table 2: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — Microchip MCP6004-I/P.Quad rail-to-rail op-amp, 14-PDIP; approximately $0.60 each.DigiKey product. Operates from 1.8–6 V• Compatible with 5 V rail• Rail-to-rail input/output• Four amplifier channels• Low ~100 µA typical current per channel. Four channels may be unnecessary• 1 MHz gain-bandwidth product• 14-pin DIP requires more PCB space. Option 2 — Microchip MCP6002-I/P.Dual rail-to-rail op-amp, 8-PDIP; approximately $0.45 each.DigiKey product. Same 1.8–6 V supply range• Smaller and less expensive• Low power consumption. Only two channels• Requires schematic and pinout changes• Limited high-frequency performance. Option 3 — Texas Instruments LM324AN.Quad general-purpose op-amp, 14-PDIP; approximately $0.57 each.DigiKey product. Four channels• Inexpensive• Familiar architecture• Single-supply operation. Output is not rail-to-rail• Higher input bias current• Reduced signal swing near positive supply rail.

docs.title: Selected Operational Amplifier
docs.text:
Choice: Option 1 — MCP6004.

The MCP6004 supports operation from the regulated 5 V rail and provides rail-to-rail input/output capability.

Its low current consumption and four available amplifier channels make it suitable for conditioning the microphone signal before conversion by the PIC ADC.

The additional channels provide flexibility for amplification and filtering.

The final component package and PCB footprint must match the selected manufacturing method.

Photo note: Images for options 2 and 3 are representative package photographs.

docs.title: 3. Power Regulation
docs.text:
5 V Voltage Regulator

The block diagram specifies a 9 V, 3 A unregulated source and a regulated 5 V, 1.5 A output.

The microphone requires an additional supply below 3.6 V.

Table 3: Component selection comparison

Solution Pros Cons Option 1 — STMicroelectronics L7805CV.5 V linear regulator, TO-220, nominal 1.5 A; approximately $1.08 each.DigiKey product. Meets nominal 5 V / 1.5 A target• Simple linear design• Through-hole package• Thermal protection. Dissipates heat proportional to input-output voltage difference• 6 W dissipation at 1.5 A from 9 V• Does not provide 3.3 V microphone supply. Option 2 — Traco Power TSR 1-2450.5 V switching regulator, 1 A maximum; approximately $6.28 each.DigiKey product. Lower heat dissipation• Wide 6.5–36 V input range• Convenient 3-pin package. Only 1 A maximum• Higher cost• Switching noise may require additional filtering.

docs.title: Selected Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
Choice (provisional): Option 1 — L7805CV.

The L7805CV meets the nominal 5 V, 1.5 A requirement and provides a straightforward linear regulation solution.

However, the regulator's current rating does not guarantee full-load operation without adequate thermal management.

At 9 V input and 1.5 A output:

\[ P = (9 - 5)(1.5) = 6\text{ W} \]

The actual microphone subsystem current is expected to be substantially lower. The final current requirement will be determined through the power budget.

docs.title: Additional 3.3 V Regulation
docs.text:
The selected microphone requires a lower-voltage supply.

A possible regulator is the STMicroelectronics LD1117V33, which provides a nominal 3.3 V output.

DigiKey product

The regulator selection remains provisional until the power architecture and required capacitors are verified.

docs.title: 4. Interface and Power Considerations
docs.text: The microphone subsystem interfaces with the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano and the other team subsystems.

docs.title: Signal Path
docs.text:
1. The analog MEMS microphone detects acoustic signals.
  2. The MCP6004 operational amplifier conditions the microphone output.
  3. The conditioned signal is connected to RA0.
  4. The PIC ADC converts the analog signal into digital data.
  5. The microcontroller processes the signal and communicates with the other subsystems.

docs.title: Power Requirements
docs.text:
• External supply: 9 V DC nominal.
  • Main regulated supply: 5 V.
  • Microphone supply: 3.3 V proposed.
  • Operational amplifier: 5 V.
  • PIC18F57Q43: powered according to the Curiosity Nano configuration.

The power budget must account for the microcontroller, microphone, amplifier, regulator quiescent currents, and additional powered components.

A 25% current margin will be included in the power calculations.

docs.title: PCB Considerations
docs.text:
The selected microphone uses a bottom acoustic port.

The PCB design must include the appropriate acoustic opening and manufacturer-recommended footprint.

The final design must also address the team's rechargeable-power requirement.

docs.title: Microcontroller Configuration
docs.text:
The Microchip PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano was configured using MPLAB Code Configurator (MCC) in MPLAB X IDE v6.35.

MCC was used to assign the analog and digital pins required for microphone signal acquisition, pushbutton input, LED control, and communication with other team subsystems.

The following peripherals were configured:

  • ADC: Analog input for microphone signal acquisition.
  • DAC1: Analog output on RA2.
  • UART1: Serial communication with other team subsystems.
  • GPIO: Digital inputs and outputs for the interrupt signal, pushbutton, and LED.

docs.title: UART Configuration
docs.text:
UART1 was configured with the following settings:

Parameter Configuration Peripheral UART1 Baud rate 9600 Parity None TX pin RC6 RX pin RC7 Team connector TX Pin 3 Team connector RX Pin 4

The UART pin assignments follow the team's agreed connector configuration.

docs.title: MCC Pin Assignments
docs.text:
Table 4: PIC18F57Q43 MCC pin configuration

PIC Pin Peripheral Direction Custom Name Function RA0 ADC Input IO_RA0 Microphone analog input RA1 GPIO Output INT_OUT Interrupt output RA2 DAC1 Output IO_RA2 Analog output RC6 UART1 Output IO_RC6 UART transmit RC7 UART1 Input IO_RC7 UART receive RD1 GPIO Input BUTTON Pushbutton RD2 GPIO Output RED_LED Red LED

RA0 and RA2 are configured as analog pins.

The UART and GPIO pins are configured as digital signals.

docs.title: MCC Pin Configuration Screenshot
docs.text: The following screenshot shows the configured PIC18F57Q43 pins in MPLAB Code Configurator.

docs.title: Configuration Summary
docs.text:
The MCC configuration establishes the microcontroller pin assignments for the microphone detection subsystem.

The ADC receives the conditioned microphone signal through RA0. UART1 provides communication through RC6 and RC7.

RA1 provides a digital interrupt output, RD1 receives the pushbutton input, and RD2 controls the red LED.

The configuration was created in the Microphone_Lab project using MPLAB Code Configurator.

Firmware operation and complete hardware integration will require further verification.

docs.title: Conclusion
docs.text:
The selected microphone candidate is the 3SM121MZB1UA, which provides 66 dBA signal-to-noise ratio, low current consumption, and a single-ended analog output.

The MCP6004 was selected for signal conditioning because of its low-power operation, rail-to-rail capability, and compatibility with the regulated 5 V supply.

The L7805CV is the preliminary 5 V voltage regulator selection.

The PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano was configured in MCC with ADC, DAC, UART, and GPIO functions required for the microphone subsystem.

The remaining design considerations include finalizing the microphone's 3.3 V supply, confirming PCB footprints, and verifying the complete circuit.

docs.title: Power Budget — Microphone Subsystem
docs.text: EGR 304 | Team 203

docs.title: Overview
docs.text:
The microphone subsystem uses a 9–12 V DC input and an LM7805 linear voltage regulator to provide a regulated 5 V power rail. This rail supplies the PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano development board and the microphone signal-conditioning circuit.

The following power budget is preliminary. Current values are design estimates pending verification against the final component datasheets.

docs.title: Section A — Component Current Requirements
docs.text:
Component Supply Voltage Estimated Current PIC18F57Q43 Curiosity Nano 5 V input 100 mA MCP6004 operational amplifier 5 V 5 mA Microphone circuit 5 V 1 mA Total 106 mA

The values above are preliminary allowances, not confirmed absolute maximum currents. Additional small loads, including the indicator LED, must be checked before finalizing the budget.

docs.title: Section B — Power Rail and Safety Margin
docs.text:
The subsystem uses one regulated 5 V rail.

Parameter Value Estimated component current 106 mA Required safety margin 25% Safety margin current 26.5 mA Estimated current requirement 132.5 mA Estimated 5 V load power 0.6625 W

The 25% safety margin is applied to the estimated operating current:

106 mA × 1.25 = 132.5 mA

docs.title: Section C — Voltage Regulator
docs.text:
The selected regulator is the LM7805 linear voltage regulator.

  • Input: 9–12 V DC
  • Regulated output: 5 V DC
  • Regulator output current requirement: approximately 133 mA, based on preliminary estimates

At the maximum 12 V input, estimated regulator power dissipation is:

P = (12 V - 5 V) × 0.1325 A

P = 0.9275 W

This is a preliminary conservative calculation using the margin-adjusted current. Thermal performance must be checked before final PCB fabrication.

docs.title: Section D — External Power Source
docs.text:
The subsystem is designed to use an external 9–12 V DC supply through a barrel jack.

The final power supply must support the subsystem's maximum current requirements with the specified safety margin. A specific adapter's rated output current must be confirmed before calculating remaining available current.

docs.title: Section E — Battery Life
docs.text: Battery life is not applicable because the current design uses an external DC power supply rather than a battery.

docs.title: Design Conclusions
docs.text:
The preliminary budget indicates that the microphone subsystem has relatively modest power requirements. A single regulated 5 V rail simplifies the design and reduces the number of required power components.

The primary concern identified is heat dissipation in the LM7805 regulator, particularly when operating from a 12 V input.

Before finalizing the design, the maximum current consumption of each active component, the complete load current, the selected adapter's current rating, and the regulator's thermal performance will be verified.

docs.title: Microphone Signal Conditioning
docs.text:
The microphone detects acoustic signals and provides an electrical signal to the MCP6004 operational amplifier.

The amplifier conditions the microphone signal before it reaches the microcontroller's analog-to-digital converter (ADC).

A 10 kΩ multiturn potentiometer provides an adjustable reference voltage for the amplifier.

The potentiometer is adjusted to approximately 2.5 V to establish the desired reference level.

docs.text:
The subsystem uses an external 9–12 V DC supply.

An LM7805 linear voltage regulator provides a regulated 5 V supply for the circuit.

The design uses a single regulated 5 V power rail.

The 10 kΩ potentiometer establishes an adjustable reference voltage of approximately 2.5 V for the amplifier.

No additional 3.3 V regulator is required for the selected design.

docs.title: Signal Flow
docs.text:
1. The class-supplied microphone detects sound.
  2. The MCP6004 amplifies and conditions the microphone signal.
  3. The 10 kΩ potentiometer establishes the amplifier reference voltage.
  4. The conditioned signal enters the PIC18F57Q43 through RA0.
  5. The microcontroller processes the ADC readings.
  6. UART1 provides communication with the other team subsystems.
